intent: The spot in the ocean farthest from any land, so remote that astronauts overhead are often the closest people, and the reason space agencies aim dead satellites at it.
pacing_profile: documentary: cold open, place, why in 2–5 beats, twist, close answers the open, short CTA (docs/STORY_GUIDELINES.md §2)
pause_policy: Pause only at the marked ellipses.
title: The place where the nearest people are in space

lines.direction: the opening line, cold — the map is already moving
lines.text: There is a point in the ocean where the nearest human beings are usually in orbit.

lines.direction: pull back; the empty circle draws on 'farthest'; counter on the distance
lines.text: This is Point Nemo, the spot in the South Pacific farthest from any land. The nearest coast is 2,688 kilometres away.

lines.direction: three pins land on their names; three spokes draw from the centre
lines.text: Three specks of land sit on that circle: Ducie Island to the north, Motu Nui off Easter Island to the north-east, and Maher Island, on the edge of Antarctica, to the south.

lines.direction: tighten back onto the point; satellite sticker arcs over on 'station'; card with the altitude
lines.text: Nobody lives on any of them. The space station passes about 400 kilometres overhead, so when it does, its crew are the closest people to this spot.

lines.direction: the circle fills; counter of spacecraft on 'hundred'; the sticker falls in
lines.text: That emptiness is useful. Space agencies steer dead spacecraft to burn up and fall here, more than 250 of them so far, including the Mir space station.

lines.direction: answer the opening line with the same noun
lines.text: The loneliest point in the ocean, where the only neighbours pass by in orbit.

lines.direction: short follow — the outro visual does the work
lines.text: Follow for a new map story every day.
